issues.failure_explanation: Theorem theo:evolND shows only that X(t) satisfies (e:sylvesterNDC). This is a necessary condition, obtained after multiplying by the Kronecker-sum matrix A. X(t) can be recovered from it only when the Sylvester operator is nonsingular, i.e., when every sum of one eigenvalue from each A_j is nonzero (Section 2). If some sum vanishes, the equation does not determine X(t), and the solver divides by zero. Simplest example: all A_j = 0. Then X(t) = X(0) + tB, but (e:sylvesterNDC) reduces to 0 = 0. The abstract and introduction claim the method works for any constant-coefficient linear system, at any t, without this hypothesis.

failure_location.quote: As an important application, the method allows to compute the solution of linear $N$-dimensional systems of ODEs of constant coefficients at any time $t$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis that all eigenvalue sums are nonzero (A nonsingular) to the application claims and to the use of Theorem theo:evolND and evolND.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised generality of the ODE/PDE application is unsupported for singular operators. The theorem itself, as a statement that X(t) satisfies the equation, remains true. The paper's experiments satisfy the hypothesis.
issues.title: ODE application claimed for all constant-coefficient systems, but it needs a nonsingular Kronecker-sum operator
issues.why_classification: A single standard solvability hypothesis, already identified in Section 2, fixes the claim. It excludes only the degenerate singular case; the theorem, method and all reported experiments are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: has a unique solution $\X\in\CC^{n_1\times n_2}$, if and only if $\sigma(\A_1) \cap \sigma(-\A_2) = \emptyset$
In what regards the uniqueness of the solution, the coefficients are uniquely determined from \eqref{e:yi1i2iN} in a recursive way.

issues.failure_explanation: The nonzero-eigenvalue-sum condition characterizes unique solvability for every right-hand side, i.e., nonsingularity of the Kronecker sum. It does not characterize existence for a given B. Counterexample: B = 0 always has the solution X = 0, even when some eigenvalue sum vanishes. More generally, any B in the range of a singular operator yields non-unique solutions. The back-substitution argument proves only sufficiency, so the 'only if' direction is false.

failure_location.quote: Therefore, \eqref{e:sylvesterND} and \eqref{e:TjYC} have a solution if and only if, when taking an eigenvalue of each matrix $\A_j$, their sum is always different from zero

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate as: the equations have a unique solution for every B if and only if all eigenvalue sums are nonzero.
issues.overall_effect: The stated existence criterion is incorrect as written. The algorithm, which assumes nonzero denominators, is unaffected.
issues.title: False 'only if' existence claim for the N-dimensional Sylvester equation
issues.why_classification: A local rewording gives the correct statement. No method, result or guarantee depends on the false direction.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we need one division, $(n_1 - i_1) + (n_2 - i_2) + \ldots + (n_N - i_N)$ products in the numerator
We explain carefully all the steps, and calculate accurately the computational cost required.

issues.failure_explanation: Write P = n_1...n_N and S = sum of n_j. Each entry of Y needs one division, so there are P divisions, not N*P. Separately, even with the stated components the sum is wrong: (P/2)(5S-N) + (P/2)(5S-3N-2) + PN = P(5S-N-1), not P(5S-N+1). With the correct division count the total is P(5S-2N). The leading term 5Nn^{N+1} is unaffected.

failure_location.quote: Therefore, in order to fully determine $\Y$, we need $n_1n_2\ldots n_NN$ divisions

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Count P divisions and redo the summation, giving a total of P(5S - 2N) flops plus the Schur decompositions.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised 'accurate' exact flop count is wrong in its lower-order terms. The asymptotic cost and the O(n^{N+1}) conclusion survive.
issues.title: Exact operation count is internally inconsistent (division count and final summation)
issues.why_classification: Routine recomputation fixes the count. The leading-order cost, the method and all conclusions are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Moreover, the solution of \eqref{e:uxt} is $u(\xx, t) = (1+\exp(t))\exp(-\xx\cdot\xx)$.
The solution at $t = 1$, taking $N = 6$ dimensions, took $25.73$ seconds to execute, and the error was $9.6811\times10^{-14}$

issues.failure_explanation: Let g = exp(-x.x). Then Lap g = (4|x|^2 - 2N)g and 2x.grad g = -4|x|^2 g, so Lap g + 2x.grad g + (2N+1)g = g. For u = a(t)g the PDE reduces to a' = a - 1, so a(t) = 1 + C e^t. The claimed solution has a(0) = 2, which contradicts u(x,0) = g. With the stated initial datum the solution is the stationary u = g. Hence the reference solution used to measure the error does not solve the problem as stated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the initial condition to u(x,0) = 2exp(-x.x), which is consistent with the claimed solution. Alternatively, take u = exp(-x.x) as the (stationary) reference solution.
issues.overall_effect: The stated test problem and its claimed exact solution are inconsistent, so the reported accuracy is not verified against the problem as written.
issues.title: Claimed exact solution of the advection-diffusion test violates the stated initial condition
issues.why_classification: A one-line correction of the initial datum makes problem and solution consistent, leaving the method and the numerical test intact.
